title: Founders Should Avoid Bad Investors: how to spot them and what good ones do
summary: Dalton Caldwell and PB (Standard Capital) explain what separates good from bad angel investors. Bad ones fear loss, slow-walk diligence, try to control founders and often have no real budget; good ones move fast, diversify and accept most bets go to zero. Includes concrete screening questions for founders.

principles.text: Judge an investor by their actual track record: ask how many investments they made last year, check sizes, and call those founders.
principles.quote: how many other investments have you made in the past year, how big were the checks, and what were they? And then you could contact you know, you could like look if it's on the website that's fine, but you could contact those people

principles.text: Many bad investors have no money or a tiny budget; they meet hundreds of founders to make one investment or try to act as middlemen.
principles.quote: They're just trying to insert themselves as a middleman between someone with money and a startup.

principles.text: Slow fundraising processes are a bad sign and cause adverse selection: only founders with no alternatives tolerate slow investors.
principles.quote: the slowest investors have the worst returns.

principles.text: Sophisticated investors keep their process light; elaborate process is a sign of inexperience.
principles.quote: The sign of a good investor is often that their process is great. Um because it means they're sophisticated.

principles.text: Early-stage investing rewards diversification: spread across many checks rather than one big bet, since outcomes are inherently unpredictable.
principles.quote: you want to split up the number of checks you you write. It's like you get to roll the dice.

principles.text: Good investors write the check, then mentally kiss the money goodbye; panic, clawing money back or micromanaging founders hurts the company.
principles.quote: you write the check and then step two is you kiss the money goodbye.
